query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A nanocrystalline high‐entropy alloy coating based on the AlCoCrFeNi system (with or without minor alloying additions such as Ti to further promote protective oxide formation) can be deposited onto a copper substrate to create a strongly adherent, ultrahard surface layer that significantly reduces wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A copper matrix (or copper substrate) with its native surface finish.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin film (via methods such as sputtering or spark plasma sintering–assisted deposition) of an AlCoCrFeNi-based high‐entropy alloy onto the copper surface.
generation.conditions: Room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures during deposition and subsequent wear testing under reciprocating or sliding conditions in ambient air.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, nanocrystalline microstructure in the HEA coating that, under service conditions, develops a continuous protective oxide layer (e.g. combinations of Al2O3, Cr2O3, or spinel phases) at the surface.
generation.mechanism: The severe lattice distortion inherent to the HEA promotes high hardness and, under mechanical action, tribo‐oxidation; the resulting protective oxide film reduces abrasion and improves wear resistance while a favorable microstructure and relatively compatible thermal expansion help ensure strong adhesion to the copper substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the uncoated copper, the Cu substrate with the HEA coating will show a significantly lower wear rate, increased surface hardness, and good adhesion with no premature delamination during wear testing.
generation.baseline: A bare copper surface that exhibits low hardness and high wear rate in tribological applications.
generation.boundary: This outcome is expected under standard ambient atmosphere wear tests and moderate service temperatures where the deposition process yields minimal interfacial reaction; extreme thermal cycling or very high temperature conditions may challenge the adhesion and raise uncertainties.
generation.uncertainty: Precise adhesion strength and long‐term interfacial stability between the HEA coating and copper need to be verified, as the mismatch in thermal expansion and potential interdiffusion at the interface could affect performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of copper substrates: one set will be coated with a sputtered or plasma‐assisted deposited nanocrystalline AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA film (with or without minor Ti addition), and the other set will remain uncoated. Subject both sets to identical reciprocating wear and micro-scratch adhesion tests under ambient conditions. Analyze cross-sectional microstructures (using SEM/EDS) to verify the formation of the protective oxide layer and interface quality.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate (mass loss or wear scar dimensions) using tribometry
Microhardness of the coating and substrate via nanoindentation
Adhesion strength determined by micro-scratch or pull-off tests
Microstructural and chemical analysis of the coating and interface (e.g., by SEM/EDS and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA-coated copper does not display a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and an improvement in surface hardness compared to bare copper, or if the coating shows poor adhesion (e.g., extensive delamination during testing), then the hypothesis that the AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA coating enhances wear resistance on a Cu substrate will be falsified.

Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
